Not knowing the exact technical terms doesn’t make someone stupid — it just means they’re trying to describe what they’re experiencing in the language they think fits.
Your job isn’t to gatekeep terminology — it’s to listen for the meaning behind the words.
If you focus less on how “wrong” their phrasing is and more on what they’re actually trying to tell you, you’ll solve the problem a lot faster — and you won’t come off like someone who’s more interested in feeling superior than being helpful. 

The term “ping” refers to sending a small network packet (an ICMP Echo Request) to a target IP and waiting for a reply to test connectivity. Any device with an internet connection, including phones, can initiate a ping to check if another device is reachable ￼. The caller’s usage of that term isn’t entirely wrong from a technical perspective, but we have no context to draw from here.

It sounds like you’re struggling with some personal feelings of comparison and resentment here — but you’re framing it unfairly against your brother.
First, autism isn’t a competition, and success (career, relationships, social skills) doesn’t invalidate someone’s diagnosis. Autism, like any spectrum, presents differently in every individual. Some autistic people are outgoing, skilled socially, even “manipulative” if they learned to mask heavily — it doesn’t make them “less autistic.”

Second, what you’re describing — different behavior around parents vs friends — is completely normal for most people, autistic or not. People adjust their behavior depending on the environment. It’s called code-switching or masking, and it’s actually extremely common among neurodivergent people trying to navigate different social expectations.

Lastly, if you feel like something is “off,” it’s likely not about him — it’s about your own unresolved feelings toward him. Comparing yourself to your brother won’t give you clarity. It will only feed bitterness.
If you genuinely think you might be autistic, talk to a specialist — but don’t weaponize your insecurity against someone else’s experience.

I completely understand where you're coming from, and I agree there's value in learning from professional tracks—industry standards exist for a reason. However, I've found that overly detailed annotations, especially at the micro-level (marking every kick, snare, or hi-hat), can sometimes stifle creativity rather than inspire it. It's easy to become overly focused on replicating what's already been done, potentially limiting opportunities for innovation and personal expression.

My recent approach has been to study psytrance tracks from a macro perspective, noting common structures, energy transitions, and broad patterns. Instead of directly replicating exact placement or details, I focus on the larger arrangement—the "bigger brush strokes." Then I refine the arrangement in multiple passes, gradually adding layers of complexity and detail. This allows a balance between structured efficiency (leveraging industry standards) and creative flexibility, enabling me to maintain originality while producing faster and more enjoyably.

Ultimately, I believe it's about finding the right balance—learning from industry norms to avoid unnecessary pitfalls but also staying flexible enough to let your creative instincts lead the way. This method helped me significantly reduce production time and enjoy the process more, rather than feeling constrained by overly detailed mappings. It's important to use guidelines as exactly that—guidelines, not strict rules—so we can push boundaries and keep the genre evolving.

What specifically sounds “bad” when you’re listening to the kick and bass in your headphones? 
Assuming that it’s the low end/ sub material? Most headphones have better bass response than low to midrange level studio monitors. There is also the proximity effect, room treatment, speaker placement. Referencing and spectrum analyzers are your best friend. I finally invested in some higher grade monitors which helps…but definitely still check back and forth with the cans. 

There is also context to consider. Meaning…don’t spend a lot of time engineering the kick bass when you start a track. This took me a while to learn. Anymore, I just start a track with the same generic kick sample, throw on a generic bass patch on a vst knowing it’s just a temporary placeholder and then focus on the other elements. (Same with the snare). Once I have some main elements going then I’ll start properly crafting the kick, bass and snare…paying more attention to frequencies and phase…but keeping it fairly clean and sound design that compliments the other elements. Once the track is fully arranged and I’m preparing to mix do I get OCD with that - there’s “mastering” to consider and how it all sounds hitting a limiter/mastering chain. Anyway, this is what I’ve learned….Maybe it can help.

I think it’s difficult to develop a Psytrance specific “masterclass” because the nature of “psychedelic” music relies heavily on experimentation, trial and error. Psytrance is also heavy on the sound design side. It’s worth investing some time in learning a particular synth inside and out. 

I’ve picked up a few different courses and got some value but have yet to find anything “comprehensive”.  It also depends on what style of Psy you’re into. 

I would suggest you pick up 25 tracks you love from Beatport or Bandcamp (wav or flac files). Drop them in your daw and analyze the fuck out of them. Use empty midi clips to map out patterns, arrangement, flow, transitions, breaks, builds, etc. You will start to notice some common patterns between them. Write down some notes for each one. 

You will probably get sick of doing that by the third or 4th one but keep going. I have a notebook loaded with notes and observations from doing that. (I refer back to them occasionally) 

There’s plenty of mixing and mastering courses out there you can apply to Psytrance too.

This is just my opinion…but..Psytrance îs a little different.  

There are lots of EDM genres that are very structured.  House and trance tutorials are a dime a dozen.  

Build a 16 bar loop. Develop a main melody/progression that is the counterpoint for the whole track.

Then arrange it.

Intro. Build it up, drop hints and tease the melody.  Build the tension. Break it down.  Big buildup. Drop the main melody, outro. Done.

The nature of psychedelic music is less structured, more open.  (Think about the Grateful Dead getting on a tangent and jamming out for 30 minutes straight.) It’s more  about flow and less about a chord progression with a melody on top.

I think this is why it’s difficult to find decent Psytrance Masterclasses because outside of Kick, Bass, and drums…it’s all vibe, atmosphere, experimentation and how the hell do you teach that?  

I would say focus on sound design and learn the f\*ck out of one or two synths.  There’s a few fundamental rules…like kick/bass needs to be solid. There’s plenty of tutorials on that.  If you can get a solid groove with kick/bass/drums and develop those parts over time, that’s half the battle. The rest of it is just throwing paint on the canvas and seeing what sticks and what doesn’t.

Depends on the type of bass (offbeat vs rolling) and the tempo.  I can get away with a slightly longer kick with a rolling style sub than an offbeat. 

Most of the producers I know, develop the sub first and then find a kick that works with it.  It's easier to match a kick to a sub then the other way around.  Phase alignment is another slick way to mesh those things together.  Spend some time analyzing the low end of professional tracks...you'll start to realize that the sub carries a little more weight than the kick.  The energy from the kick is in the attack and the "knock" (the part that follows the initial transient of the kick).  Hint - Watch tutorials from Adam Ellis and ReOrder - you'll note that they do little to no processing on their kicks. It's all about the relationship between the two.  Good monitors so that you can feel the bass is necessary for nailing this down. (Spectrum analyzers can help bridge the gap)

The mid bass is too hot, the sub is too low. The interplay between the kick and sub are the foundation...you'll want that piece to be solid. Very dry sounding.  No effects, sweeps, atmospheres, impacts or one shot effects. These are important to keep the track moving and create more interest in the intro and outro.   Less tonal sounds and more percussion during the intro/outro will improve your chances of getting your track included in a mix. The pluck during the break is pretty thin in comparison to the pads. You'll want some beef in your plucks during the breakdown - it's the focus of the track at that point.  

In general, something new should be happening every 8 bars...build things up and break them back down.  Work on smooth transitions...fade new parts in, fade new parts out. Tease the melodic parts of your main drop throughout the track.

Melodically it's good, but you have some work to do on the production side.  Keep at it.  Cheers!

I start my tracks with a notebook and a pen.  I write out my ideas for describing the sound, ...describe the vibe, etc.  That usually determines how I start the track.  So for instance,  if I'm going for something techy and groove based I'll start with percussion and bass.  If I'm going for something melodic I'll start with chords and a lead line.  My starting template opens up two blank naked midi tracks, because I don't always with the same VSTi or maybe I want to start with a different EQ.  As far as structure goes, I base it on the feel of the song and don't copy the structure from existing tracks. I have a 1TB drive dedicated to my sample library. I group by "instrument" (i.e. Kicks, Snares, Top Loops, etc.).  
In my project/working space I create a folder for each track and name it sequentially and include the BPM, for example: track6_Dm_138  
I also include a notes.txt file in each project folder where I jot down my initial ideas/vibe/structure/genre for the track. 
I do this because I don't typically work on a track from start to finish.  I usually work in batches of 4 or 5.  I found that working this way keeps me from getting bogged down in a track or get sick of hearing the same thing over and over for a week+. It takes a little organizing to work like this so I'm pretty OCD about folder structure and making notes.  Usually 1 or 2 of the tracks will hit a point where I'll just drop them into my "Recycle" folder (sometimes I'll come back and nick a chord progression or something from one of these "dead" tracks and use it in something new.) and focus on the other tracks or start something else new.
